text: This is fleetci. A controller takes CI jobs from GitHub and GitLab, and hands them to workers: machines that can be anywhere, in another office, a data center, or another country. Every job runs in a fresh microVM of the size it asks for.
Here, one controller and three workers, each in a different place. A worker only needs to reach the controller over the network, whether it is one hop away or a continent away.
On the controller, fleetci init creates the fleet's certificate authority, and the controller's own certificate. Every machine in the fleet proves who it is with a certificate from it.
Then the controller starts. Its config names the GitHub organization and the GitLab runner it takes jobs from. Several controllers would elect a leader; this one leads on its own.
To add a machine, the controller issues a join token, good for a single join, so each worker gets its own. Then this pane watches the fleet.
Each worker joins with one command. It gets its certificate from the controller, and the binaries it runs VMs with, so fleetci is all it needs to start with.
Before taking a job, a worker boots a microVM of each class it offers, checks that a job can run in it, and keeps a snapshot, so later VMs start in a couple of seconds.
All three are Ready, each with its budget, and room for so many VMs of each class.
Now the jobs: two GitHub workflows, and a GitLab pipeline. Nine jobs, more than the fleet has room for at once.

The leader places each job on a worker with room, filling the busiest first, so the others stay free. Each job gets its own microVM, restored from the snapshot, and deleted when the job ends. Jobs that don't fit wait for a place.
All nine jobs passed, across the three workers. None of their microVMs is left.
fleetci. Per-job microVMs for GitHub and GitLab, on your own machines, wherever they are.
